deep.reconstruction:
Problem: steady efflux of water through a channel made of four straight segments AF=a, BC=b, CD=c, DE=d. Their cross-sections are ff, gg, hh, ii, and they are inclined at angles ε, ζ, η, θ to the vertical. The orifice is EE=kk. v is the height due to the efflux velocity, and l (about 30 ft of water) is the atmospheric pressure at the top AA and at the orifice. Euler's friction hypothesis (§§1–34 of E260) makes the frictional resistance proportional to the local pressure divided by a size of the section. Integrating along a uniform segment then gives exponential relaxation of the pressure. Across segment n the pressure map is affine: p_out = p_in·e^{-αL/s} + (s/α)(1−e^{-αL/s})cosφ + k^4 v(1/s^4 − 1/s'^4). The last term is the Bernoulli (continuity) jump at the junction, since velocity ∝ k²/s². The previous page wrote these four maps and closed the chain with the orifice condition (outlet pressure = l).

On this page (§37) Euler abbreviates e^{-αa/f} = 1−αA, etc., so that A = (1/α)(1−e^{-αa/f}) = (a/f)(1 − αa/2f + α²a²/6f² − α³a³/24f³ + …), and similarly for B, C, D. Then (f/α)(1−e^{-αa/f}) = Af.

§38 composes the affine maps:
- P = (1−αA)l + Af + k^4v(1/f^4−1/g^4).
- Q = (1−αA)(1−αB)l + (1−αB)Af + Bg cosζ + (1−αB)k^4v/f^4 + αB k^4v/g^4 − k^4v/h^4.
- R = (1−αA)(1−αB)(1−αC)l + A(1−αB)(1−αC)f + B(1−αC)g cosζ + Ch cosη + (1−αB)(1−αC)k^4v/f^4 + αB(1−αC)k^4v/g^4 + αC k^4v/h^4 − k^4v/i^4.

The orifice condition l = R(1−αD) + Di cosθ + k^4v(1/i^4 − 1/k^4) then gives one linear equation in v. It is begun here and finished on p.352; §39 solves it explicitly for v.

So the page is the bookkeeping that turns a product of affine segment-maps into a closed formula for the discharge. Euler remarks this gives the general rule for a channel of any number of parts.
errors: No error on this page: the expansions of A–D and the compositions giving Q and R check out term by term.

The first segment's gravity term is written Af with no cos ε (also on p.350). This tacitly takes the top segment as vertical (ε=0), consistent with p.352's head a + b cosζ + …. Strictly it should be Af cosε if ε≠0.
Continuation (p.352, outside this page): the term αB(1−αC)(1−αD)k^4v/h^4 should have g^4 in the denominator.
Also on p.352, in the §39 numerator 𝔄𝔅ℭ𝔇𝔣 should read 𝔄𝔅ℭ𝔇·l.

Physical caveat, not algebraic: the pressure-proportional friction law makes the discharge depend on atmospheric pressure l. This is an artefact of Euler's hypothesis and is not borne out by experiment.

ideas.what: Friction proportional to pressure in a uniform pipe yields exponential decay of the pressure along each segment, written as 1 − αA with A given by its power series in α.
ideas.modern_name: Exponential (capstan-type) law from pressure-proportional Coulomb-like friction; linear ODE solution
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (rope/capstan friction, Euler–Eytelwein formula); hydraulic version is E260 itself
ideas.where_published: E260 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 6, 1761); capstan analogue in Euler's rope-friction memoir (Mém. Berlin 1762)

ideas.what: Composition of segment-wise affine pressure maps, including Bernoulli jumps at junctions, to get the discharge of a compound pipe.
ideas.modern_name: Series composition / transfer-map method for pipes in series (head-loss bookkeeping)

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine algebra within a known (and physically superseded) Euler friction model. It is correct and already in print in E260, so there is nothing a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: In the expansion of B, the image shows the denominator as '2 g' (a print blemish resembling '1 g'); 2g is correct, as transcribed.
The last line in the image is A(1−αB)(1−αC)(1−αD)f; a blot makes the second factor look like (1+αC), but the minus sign is intended. The transcription is correct.
